_metadata.description: Retrieval eval set for doc_type="book" (docs/DESIGN-book-chapters-and-hierarchy.md Part 3 Step 1, extended per docs/PLAN-book-rag-experiments.md §1 "Experiment 0"): 40 questions, 8 per book, across all 5 ingested books -- local:14b7e283bdcd (Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments, no PDF outline, 16 chapter units), local:f0929288d4f3 (Causal Inference in Python, a 223-entry/4-level PDF outline the splitter does not yet use, 26 chapter units), local:f6c64e1e8c7d (Elements of Causal Inference, 8 chapter units), local:dfe850b3281a (Causal Inference and Discovery in Python, 7 chapter units), local:54d6ca71dda9 (Causal Inference and Machine Learning in Economics, Social, and Health Sciences, 44 chapter units). All 5 use today's Strategy B size-merge split (rag/book_summarizer.py's _split_chapters(), unmodified). This is the eval set Experiment 0 runs app/retrieval_eval.py against to produce the first 5-book baseline; earlier revisions of this file covered only the first 2 books (15 questions) as a format proof before scaling to the full set.
_metadata.structure: Array of self-contained records keyed by question_id (same self-contained shape as eval_equation_slice.json -- no blind-file split; this is a small authored slice, not the imported 210-question set). Each record carries BOTH scoring grounds: gold_chapter_title (scored against PaperSearchResult.chapter from search_papers/Retriever.retrieve_papers -- chapter-ROUTING accuracy) and gold_block_id (scored against GroundedResult.anchor.block_id from semantic_search/Retriever.retrieve -- passage RECALL). They measure different things per the design doc: chapter routing is what ChapterSummary/book_summarizer.py exist for; passage recall is whether chapter work affects retrieval at all or only navigation. gold_block_id/gold_chunk_id are the CHUNK's real anchor block (rag/chunker.py's _build_chunk: anchor.block_id always pins a chunk's FIRST block, never the block that happens to carry the quoted fact) -- same convention eval_equation_slice.json already uses and for the same reason: a passage-level check against the wrong (fact-carrying, non-anchor) block is unwinnable by construction, not a retrieval miss. excerpt_block_id/section_path/page/passage_excerpt describe the actual fact block instead, for human re-verification.
_metadata.authoring_method: For each of the 5 books, chapters were sampled across the full chapter range (not just the first/last -- see 'sampling_note' below) and read directly from two read-only sources against papers.db (file:...?mode=ro, uri=True -- no write, no ingest/rechunk tool run): (1) the persisted ChapterSummary.text/title rows in the summaries table, to find a chapter with a concrete, quotable fact (a number, a named theorem/law/assumption, a specific claim); (2) that chapter's own source blocks (rag/book_summarizer.py's _split_chapters(), called read-only against the live blocks table -- NOT modified -- to reproduce today's exact block-to-chapter grouping). The recomputed split was cross-checked against the persisted ChapterSummary titles for ALL 101 chapter units across all 5 books (not just the 40 units a question was drawn from): 99/101 matched exactly; the 2 mismatches are both book-opening (front-matter) units where summarize_book()'s LLM-generated-title fallback ran in production (the recomputed split's own heading-derived title was empty) -- no question in this file draws its gold_chapter_title from either of those 2 units; the persisted (production) title is what's recorded here in every case, not the recomputed one, since that's what search_papers/retrieve_papers actually returns. A question was written from the quoted block's content and the answer chapter recorded BEFORE any retrieval call was made against the corpus for that question -- no question in this file, across either authoring pass, was written by looking at what search_papers/semantic_search returns. excerpt_block_id/section_path/page/passage_excerpt are direct, verbatim provenance (including this corpus's known OCR ligature artifacts, e.g. 'diference' for 'difference', 'suficiency' for 'sufficiency' -- left uncorrected so the field stays a true substring of the live block text, matching this file's own convention already visible in the original 15, e.g. QB-013's 'Diference-in-Diferences') for re-verifying a question by hand later; gold_chunk_id/gold_block_id were then derived (also read-only) as that excerpt block's owning chunk's real anchor, using rag/chunker.py's actual Chunker class against the same reconstructed blocks -- cross-checked against the live chunks table's anchor_json for every one of the 40 questions (100% match, 0 corrections needed) -- see 'structure' above for why the anchor (not the fact block) is scored.
_metadata.chapter_split_note: gold_chapter_title and gold_block_id->chapter membership all reflect TODAY's chapter split only (rag/book_summarizer.py's Strategy B size-merge / Strategy A marker-split, unchanged by this task -- 8/7/44/26/16 units for local:f6c64e1e8c7d/local:dfe850b3281a/local:54d6ca71dda9/local:f0929288d4f3/local:14b7e283bdcd respectively, 101 total). After a future re-split (A1 PDF-outline-based or a repaired A2), gold_block_id's underlying block_id/page/text stay valid (the chunker/parser are untouched), but gold_chapter_title -- and which chapter INDEX a block falls under -- must be re-derived against the new split, not assumed to carry over; that re-derivation is exactly what Experiment 1's A/B needs this same block-level provenance for.
_metadata.doc_type_note: Every record here carries doc_type="book" and is additionally scoped by source_paper_id to one of exactly 5 paper_ids -- app/retrieval_eval.py's Question.doc_type/gold_chapter_title fields default to "paper"/None, so this file is a strict addition to the existing schema, not a fork of it (pointing the harness at eval_ground_truth.json or eval_equation_slice.json is unaffected).
_metadata.sampling_note: local:dfe850b3281a (7 chapter units) and local:54d6ca71dda9 (44 chapter units) both have irregular splits worth recording explicitly since they shaped which chapters questions could come from: dfe850b3281a's units 0-2 are front matter/table-of-contents only (no checkable book content -- unit 0 is copyright/foreword/acknowledgments, units 1-2 are literally a table-of-contents block dump), so all 8 of its questions were drawn from units 3-6 (the book's real Part 2/Part 3 content), each covering a wide page range (per-book pages ~74-437) rather than one question per unit. Separately, dfe850b3281a's chapter-marker heuristic (Strategy A, _split_by_markers) produced two PAIRS of units sharing an identical persisted title: units 2 and 5 are both titled 'Part 2: Causal Inference', and units 3 and 6 are both titled 'Part 3: Causal Discovery' -- a real chapter-level-scoring ambiguity (search_papers' chapter-routing hit check is title-string equality, so it cannot in general distinguish two same-titled chapters of the same paper_id). None of this file's 8 dfe850b3281a questions are drawn from unit 2 or unit 3, so no individual question here is scored against an ambiguous title, but a future consumer of this book's chapter-routing numbers should know the ambiguity exists in the underlying data. local:54d6ca71dda9 over-splits into 44 units because a numbered algorithm-step list (e.g., '2. Define Gini Index for a Node t') false-positive-matches the chapter-marker regex; many units are 2-13 blocks long. Questions were still drawn from across the full unit range (0, 2, 7, 24, 28, 34, 39, 43 of 0-43), including one of these small fragment-units (unit 7), since its content (a decision-tree stopping criterion) was independently a concrete, checkable fact and its inclusion documents this book's over-split behavior rather than hiding it -- directly relevant to Experiment 1's chapter-routing comparison.

ground_truth.question_text: What key insight did Amazon reach about its e-mail campaign OEC that was based on click-through revenue?
ground_truth.answer_text: That the click-through revenue OEC was optimizing for short-term revenue instead of user lifetime value -- annoyed users unsubscribe, and Amazon then loses the opportunity to target them in the future.

ground_truth.question_text: Why does the book call controlled experiments the gold standard for assessing causality?
ground_truth.answer_text: With random assignment of units to variants, the observed Treatment-vs-Control difference is the causal effect, because the second (selection-bias) term has an expected value of zero.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Trustworthy online controlled expirements_ A practical guide AB testing
ground_truth.section_path: When Controlled Experiments Are Not Possible
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Controlled experiments are the gold standard for assessing causality because, with random assignment of units to variants, the first term is the observed difference between Treatment and Control and the second term has an expected value of zero.

ground_truth.question_text: What fraction of users does the book recommend holding out in a long-term holdout ramp, and for roughly how long?
ground_truth.answer_text: A small fraction (e.g., 5-10%) of users, held out for a period such as two months.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Trustworthy online controlled expirements_ A practical guide AB testing
ground_truth.gold_chapter_title: Ramp Phase Four: Long-Term Holdout or Replication
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: we sometimes conduct a long-term holdout ramp, where a small fraction (e.g., 5–10%) of users do not receive the new Treatment for a period of time (e.g., two months) primarily for learning purposes.

ground_truth.question_text: In a correctly operating A/A test, what fraction of repeated trials should show a metric as statistically significant, per the book?
ground_truth.answer_text: About 5% of the time (p-value < 0.05), since Control and Treatment are identical.

ground_truth.passage_excerpt: If the system is operating correctly, then in repeated trials about 5% of the time a given metric should be statistically significant with p-value less than 0.05.

ground_truth.question_text: How many weeks does the book recommend running most experiments for when measuring the short-term Treatment effect?
ground_truth.answer_text: One to two weeks.

ground_truth.passage_excerpt: In most scenarios discussed in this book, we recommend running experiments for one to two weeks. The Treatment effect measured in this short timeframe is called the short-term effect.

ground_truth.question_text: What does the book call the fact that you can never observe the same unit both with and without treatment?
ground_truth.answer_text: The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference in Python_ Applying Causal Inference in the Tech Industry
ground_truth.section_path: The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: The fundamental problem of causal inference is that you can never observe the same unit with and without treatment.

ground_truth.question_text: In the book's membership-program example, why doesn't randomizing eligibility alone let you estimate the causal effect of membership itself?
ground_truth.answer_text: Because although eligibility was randomized, participation among the eligible was self-selected (more engaged customers opted in), so participants and non-participants are not comparable.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference in Python_ Applying Causal Inference in the Tech Industry
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Although the eligibility to the program was randomized, the random chunk that could opt in still self-selected into the program. In other words, randomization of program eligibility ensures that people who were able to get the program are comparable to those that weren’t. But, out of the eligible, only a fraction choose to participate.

ground_truth.question_text: In the book's three-step breakdown of the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell (FWL) theorem, what is the "debiasing step"?
ground_truth.answer_text: Regress the treatment T on the confounders X and obtain the treatment residuals T-tilde = T minus T-hat.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference in Python_ Applying Causal Inference in the Tech Industry
ground_truth.gold_chapter_title: Chapter 4. The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Linear Regression
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: 1. A debiasing step, where you regress the treatment T on confounders X and obtain the treatment residuals $\tilde { T } = T - \hat { T }$

ground_truth.question_text: According to the book, what does weighting the treated samples by 1/P(T=1|X) create?
ground_truth.answer_text: A pseudo-population the same size as the original one, but as though everyone had been treated.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference in Python_ Applying Causal Inference in the Tech Industry
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Weighting the treated samples by $1 / P ( T = 1 | X )$ creates a pseudo-population the same size as the original one, but as though everyone was treated.

ground_truth.question_text: Which real-world study does the book cite as a 2x2 DID design that challenged the theory that a minimum-wage rise reduces employment?
ground_truth.answer_text: David Card and Alan Krueger's study of fast-food restaurants in New Jersey and Pennsylvania around a New Jersey minimum-wage increase, which found no evidence of reduced employment.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference in Python_ Applying Causal Inference in the Tech Industry

ground_truth.question_text: Per the book, under what conditions does Abadie's paper argue the synthetic control method produces an unbiased ATT estimate?
ground_truth.answer_text: If the potential outcome follows either the vector autoregressive or the linear factor model, and the synthetic control matches the treated unit.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference in Python_ Applying Causal Inference in the Tech Industry
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Alberto Abadie argues that if the potential outcome follows either the vector autoregressive or the linear factor model and the synthetic control matches the treated unit, then the synthetic control method produces an unbiased estimate to the ATT.

ground_truth.question_text: How does the book define Causal Reinforcement Learning (CRL)?
ground_truth.answer_text: An area of machine learning combining causal inference and reinforcement learning, whose goal is to automate the treatment allocation process to optimize the outcome the treatment influences.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference in Python_ Applying Causal Inference in the Tech Industry
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Causal reinforcement learning (CRL) is an area of machine learning that combines the principles of causal inference and reinforcement learning. The goal of CRL is to automate the treatment allocation process with the objective of optimizing the outcome that the treatment influences.

ground_truth.question_text: What real-world example does the book give to illustrate naive Granger causality wrongly inferring that X causes Y but not vice versa?
ground_truth.answer_text: The relation between the price of butter and the price of cheese: both are strongly influenced by the price of milk, but cheese production takes much longer than butter production, causing a larger delay between the milk and cheese prices.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Elements of causal inference foundations and learning algorithms
ground_truth.section_path: Time Series > 10.3 Learning Causal Time Series Models > 10.3.3 Granger Causality
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Thus, naive application of Granger causality infers that X causes Y and Y does not cause X. This effect has been observed, for instance, for the relation between the price of butter and the price of cheese. Both prices are strongly influenced by the price of milk, but the production of cheese takes much longer than the production of butter, which causes a larger delay between the prices of milk and cheese [Peters et al., 2013, Experiment 10]. This failure of Granger causality, however, is only possible because not all relevant variables are observed, which was stated as a requirement by Granger himself.

ground_truth.gold_chapter_title: Appendix Causal Orderings and Adjacency Matrices
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Theorem B.5 The matrix A is an adjacency matrix of a DAG G if and only $i f A + { \mathrm { I d } }$ is a 0-1-matrix with all eigenvalues being real and strictly greater than zero.

ground_truth.question_text: Per the book's Lemma C.1, if X and N are independent variables and N is nondeterministic, what does the lemma conclude about N and X + N?
ground_truth.answer_text: That N is not independent of X + N.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Elements of causal inference foundations and learning algorithms
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Lemma C.1 Let X and N be independent variables and assume that N is nondeterministic. Then $N \not \vdash \left( X + N \right)$

ground_truth.question_text: In the book's collider example (a fork X, Y into a shared child B), what happens when you control for B, compared to controlling for a confounder A?
ground_truth.answer_text: Controlling for the collider B enables the flow of information between the parent variables X and Y -- the exact opposite of what happens when controlling for a confounder.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference and Discovery in Python_ Unlock the secrets of modern causal machine learning with DoWhy, EconML, PyTorch and more

ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Second, X, Y, and B form a pattern that we call a collider or immorality. This pattern has a very interesting behavior – it enables the flow of information between the parent variables (X and Y in our case) when we control for the child variable (B in our example). This is exactly the opposite of what happened when we controlled for A!

ground_truth.question_text: Per the book, what does Holland (1986) call the fact that only one potential outcome can ever be observed for a unit, and what phrase does he use to summarize it?
ground_truth.answer_text: The fundamental problem of causal inference; Holland summarized it as "No causation without manipulation."
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference and Machine Learning In Economics, Social, and Health Sciences
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Since a unit cannot exist simultaneously in both treated and untreated states, causal inference is limited by the fundamental problem of causal inference (Holland, 1986), which asserts that only one potential outcome can ever be observed. As Holland succinctly stated, “No causation without manipulation.”

ground_truth.question_text: Per the book, what four general strategies does it list for reducing overfitting?
ground_truth.answer_text: Using a simpler model, collecting more data, applying regularization, or using early stopping.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference and Machine Learning In Economics, Social, and Health Sciences
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Overfitting can be reduced by using a simpler model, collecting more data, applying regularization, or using early stopping.

ground_truth.question_text: In the book's decision-tree recursive-partitioning walkthrough, what stopping criterion does it give for insufficient Gini gain?
ground_truth.answer_text: If the maximum possible Gini Gain for any potential split falls below a certain threshold (e.g., 0.01), no further splits are made.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference and Machine Learning In Economics, Social, and Health Sciences
ground_truth.section_path: 5. Recursive Partitioning: Split Left and Right Nodes
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Insuficient Gini Gain: If the maximum possible Gini Gain (∆Gini) for any potential split falls below a certain threshold (e.g., 0.01), no further splits are made. This criterion prevents the algorithm from making splits that provide negligible improvements in class purity.

ground_truth.question_text: Per the book, what two key components make up SUTVA (the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption)?

ground_truth.question_text: Per the book, what did Abadie and Imbens (2006) develop, and why?
ground_truth.answer_text: A robust analytical method to estimate standard errors in propensity score matching (PSM), because standard bootstrapping's assumptions are violated by the discrete set of matched pairs nearest-neighbor matching produces.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference and Machine Learning In Economics, Social, and Health Sciences
ground_truth.section_path: Abadie and Imbens (2006) Correction for Standard Errors
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Recognizing the limitations of standard bootstrapping in matching settings, Abadie and Imbens (2006) developed a robust analytical method to estimate standard errors in PSM. Their approach explicitly accounts for the fact that nearest-neighbor matching leads to a discrete set of matched pairs, violating the assumptions underlying conventional variance estimators.

ground_truth.question_text: Per the book, what two procedures did Wager and Athey (2018) introduce for directly estimating heterogeneous treatment effects using causal forests?

ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Wager and Athey (2018) introduced two procedures for directly estimating heterogeneous treatment efects using causal forests. The first, known as double-sample trees (DST), builds honest trees by using separate samples for training and estimation—similar to the causal tree method we discussed earlier, but without the need for cross-validation since out-of-bag error is available. ground_truth.question_text: Per the book, what does the monotonicity assumption for instrumental variables state, and what does it rule out?
ground_truth.answer_text: That the instrument flips the treatment in only one direction -- either increasing the chance of treatment for everyone who got the instrument (no defiers) or decreasing it (no compliers).
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Causal Inference in Python_ Applying Causal Inference in the Tech Industry
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: It either increases the chance of getting the treatment for everyone who got the instrument, which is equivalent to assuming that there are no defiers; or it decreases that chance, which is equivalent to assuming that there are no compliers.
